overview: The exact atlas id “oghuz” spans 1100 to 1200, but its map is a geographic collage rather than the border of one century-long Oghuz state. The decoded polygon covers Khwarazm, Ustyurt, Mangyshlaq, and Dehistan; it excludes tested Yangikent, Jand, Sygnak, and Otrar, the lower-Syr places associated with the earlier Oghuz Yabgu world. Inside the shape, hereditary Khwarazmshahs governed oasis country, bargained with Seljuk and Qara Khitai overlords, and recruited steppe warriors. Elsewhere, distinct Oghuz communities grazed herds in upper-Oxus and Khorasan country, defeated and captured Sultan Sanjar in 1153, held cities for intervals, and followed leaders into Ghazna or Kerman. Those events never become one synchronized administration. Daily life likewise crossed social worlds: mobile herders counted wealth and obligations in animals, while Khwarazmian farmers lived around canals in multiroom mud-brick estates with hearths, storage, gardens, and sometimes puzzling towerlike buildings. Courtly Persian and Arabic writing is much easier to see than ordinary Oghuz speech, family teaching, medicine, or camp sanitation, so gaps are stated. The 1200 recoloring divides the old shape between new atlas layers; it is an editorial seam, not the extinction of Oghuz people.

periods.title: 1100 to 1127: a Khwarazmian governorship fills the map
periods.summary: The atlas begins in 1100, but Qutb al-Din Muhammad governed Khwarazm as Sanjar’s loyal vassal from 1097. Oghuz groups existed across a much wider world; this oasis government was neither a revived Yabgu state nor an administration synchronized with every community carrying the Oghuz name.

periods.title: 1127 to 1138: Atsiz inherits and tests the frontier
periods.summary: Atsiz succeeded his father in Khwarazm and initially served Sanjar. The map’s Mangyshlaq and Ustyurt side faced mobile Oghuz and Qipchaq groups, while the irrigated lower Oxus supported a hereditary court. One color therefore compresses frontier pressure, tribute, commerce, and unlike forms of power.

periods.title: 1138 to 1141: rebellion does not erase vassalage
periods.summary: Atsiz’s first open challenge brought Sanjar’s intervention and renewed submission. Political allegiance could reverse without replacing oasis households or steppe communities. This phase belongs to Khwarazmian-Seljuk rivalry inside the polygon, not to a single Oghuz ruler commanding the whole displayed region.

periods.title: 1141 to 1152: Qatwan reshapes the balance
periods.summary: Sanjar’s 1141 defeat by the Qara Khitai weakened his authority. Khwarazm remained tributary while Atsiz maneuvered and later recovered Jand. Jand tests outside the atlas Oghuz polygon, a useful warning that historical campaigning, community identity, and the software boundary are three different things.

periods.title: 1152 to 1157: Balkh falls amid a wider revolt
periods.summary: Pastoral Oghuz near Balkh chafed under taxation and official pressure. They defeated the governor outside Balkh in 1153, plundered public buildings, installed themselves in the city, and offered obedience to Sanjar’s nephew Mahmud Khan. This was local coalition rule amid wider revolt, not a replacement empire.

periods.title: 1157 to 1161: several centers claim the ruins
periods.summary: After Sanjar’s death, Khwarazm’s Il-Arslan ruled with practical independence, while Oghuz chiefs and former Seljuk commanders competed in Khorasan. No event moved authority neatly from one capital to another. The atlas label hides overlapping local coalitions, distant suzerainties, and heavily damaged cities.

periods.title: 1161 to 1165: Dehistan changes hands
periods.summary: Aytaq fled Dehistan in 1161, leaving the town to an Oghuz sack. The region later figured in Khwarazmshah campaigns in eastern Persia. This was a contested frontier: a local ruler’s flight, mobile attackers, and renewed external intervention fit no simple border line.

periods.title: 1165 to 1175: an Oghuz band holds Ghazna
periods.summary: Oghuz adventurers from Khorasan seized Ghazna around 1160 and checked Ghurid expansion for perhaps fifteen years. Ghazna lies far beyond this polygon. Their episode proves mobility and political opportunity, not a remote province of a state headquartered in the atlas-colored Khwarazm and Ustyurt zone.

periods.title: 1175 to 1187: coalitions disperse and regroup
periods.summary: The Ghazna episode ended, while Oghuz leaders remained active across Khorasan and moved toward other opportunities. Khwarazm meanwhile followed its own dynastic contests. A community’s migration or a chief’s new service did not move every Oghuz household, and no single chronology fits them all.

periods.title: 1187 to 1200: Tekish expands; the atlas prepares another seam
periods.summary: Tekish recruited northern Oghuz and Qipchaq forces and defeated the last Great Seljuk sultan in 1194. He died in 1200, exactly when the map drops “oghuz.” His dynasty expanded, yet neither his death nor the software seam marks the disappearance of Oghuz communities.

items.text: The exact live id is “oghuz,” dated approximately 1100 to 1200. It has one observed border interval and entered this work queue without a card or completed identity, chronology, or border review. The missing-card lead points to the earlier Yabgu State, which cannot simply be stretched into this century.

The sole target is a MultiPolygon with two components, three rings, and 352 coordinate positions. Its bbox runs from 50.326703267032684, 36.805078153254826 to 62.32922329223294, 49.04827397205382. The decoded geometry SHA-256 is 5cec4096b6fa0b8005292a7f5b49448abe4c78da602dc230ea13492623da9d68. These reproducible numbers describe display data, not surveyed medieval borders.

Tested Konye-Urgench, Nukus, Khiva, Dashoguz, Shetpe, Zhanaozen, Beyneu, central Ustyurt, Turkmenbashi, Balkanabat, and Dehistan fall inside. These points join an irrigated lower-Oxus oasis to plateau and Caspian-edge country; shared color does not prove that their residents answered to one Oghuz government.

Tested Yangikent, Jand, Sygnak, Otrar, Kyzylorda, Aral City, Atyrau, Saraychik, Uralsk, Merv, Bereket, Bukhara, and Samarkand fall outside. Most strikingly, the classic lower-Syr Oghuz centers Yangikent and Jand are absent. The label and shape therefore cannot be a literal Yabgu-State survival map.

The target shares encoded arcs with Cuman-Kipchak, Ghaznavid, Karakhanid, and Seljuk features. No tested point inside “oghuz” has a second owner. At 1000 the target is absent; at 1200 former member points split between Cuman and Qara Khitai layers. Boundaries and recoloring are editorial topology, not treaties or synchronized takeovers.

Qutb al-Din Muhammad governed Khwarazm as a loyal Seljuk vassal from 1097 to 1127, followed by the more independent Atsiz. That sequence governs much of the polygon’s oasis core. It is a Khwarazmshah story, not evidence for a Yabgu ruling every Oghuz group.

The 1153 rebels near Balkh had their own beys and branch organization. The cited study names separate leaders for the Üçok and Bozok groupings and describes their earlier obedience to Sanjar. Such negotiated followings fit a confederated pastoral setting better than a permanent bureaucracy covering the atlas polygon.

After Sanjar, Il-Arslan acted as an effectively independent Khwarazmshah while Oghuz chiefs, former Seljuk commanders, Qara Khitai rulers, and local claimants competed nearby. A distant overlord could receive tribute without running each market or camp. Medieval authority often stacked; the atlas gives only one paint layer.

At Balkh, Oghuz forces first aided a Ghurid occupation in 1152, then defeated Sanjar’s governor, plundered the city, offered obedience to Mahmud Khan, and held it for several years. That rapid sequence shows coalition politics and local occupation, not a stable nation-state replacing the Seljuks across Central Asia.

Around 1160, another Oghuz group took Ghazna and held it for perhaps fifteen years, while the last Ghaznavid ruled from Lahore. Ghazna is nowhere inside this target shape. The episode demonstrates how the name “Oghuz” follows people and leaders across maps rather than naming one fixed territory.

sections.title: Power, taxes, war, and political endings

items.text: The Oghuz near Balkh reportedly owed twenty-four thousand sheep annually to the Seljuk palace. Conflict escalated through an official’s coercive handling of that levy before battle in 1153. The sequence makes taxation personal and material: this was not an abstract percentage but an enormous movement of animals and authority.

Sanjar’s capture lasted roughly three years. His continued ceremonial treatment did not restore his freedom or the institutions damaged around him. He escaped in 1156 and died in 1157. The Great Seljuk political center collapsed, while households, herds, towns, and competing armed groups continued under dangerous new conditions.

Across its 1100 to 1200 slab, the atlas assigns Merv to a Ghaznavid layer rather than “oghuz,” while its Oghuz shape sits farther northwest. That mismatch is a software warning in bright colors: the political crisis most associated with twelfth-century Oghuz power lies largely outside the target polygon.

Dehistan, a tested point inside the atlas shape, gives the label one direct collision with Oghuz action: Aytaq fled in 1161 and the town was sacked. Khwarazmian power later intervened. Even here, “Oghuz” marks attackers in one episode, while restoration and local rule immediately complicate ownership.

The target disappears from the atlas at 1200, but its former points are divided between at least two successor color layers. A synchronized state-ending would need a securely dated conquest and one inheriting authority; the map supplies neither. The honest political ending is fragmentation and relabeling, not ethnic extinction.

Sheep appear in the record because officials counted tribute in them. That does not mean every family owned equal flocks or only sheep. Horses, transport animals, pasture rights, hired labor, losses, and seasonal routes remain unevenly documented. A tax total reveals state demand more clearly than it reveals a household budget.

The Balkh narrative places Oghuz pastoralists with flocks in the upper-Oxus region, where taxation and official pressure sharpened conflict. Camps had to coordinate grazing, watering, movement, and defense, but the political source does not inventory tents, cooking gear, children’s chores, or women’s property. Those daily-life details remain evidence gaps here.

Oghuz adventurers could move from Khorasan to Ghazna and seize an opening between larger powers. “Adventurers” is a political label for armed newcomers, not a description of every migrant. Their mobility may have included dependents and camp support, but the cited chronicle-based synthesis does not securely count or describe them.

The map leaves Aktau and Fort Shevchenko outside while including inland Shetpe, Zhanaozen, Beyneu, and central Ustyurt. These point tests warn against imagining the entire Mangyshlaq coast as uniformly controlled. Wells and routes mattered intensely on this dry plateau, but the polygon cannot tell us who used each one.

Mobile and settled lives were connected rather than sealed apart. Tribute animals, military recruitment, city markets, pasture disputes, and refugees carried goods and news between camps and oases. Sources usually notice the moment a herd becomes taxable or an army becomes threatening; peaceful visits and ordinary cooperation leave a fainter trail.

sections.title: Canals, farms, and houses in Khwarazm

items.text: Nerazik’s excavated rural settlements belong to Khwarazm in the twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, squarely inside much of this polygon. They document oasis residents under Khwarazmian rule, not an ethnically identified Oghuz village. That distinction lets archaeology enrich daily life without assigning every hearth an Oghuz-speaking owner.

Around Kavat-kala, excavators found estates beside canals and irrigation ditches, often combining a dwelling, garden ground, and a tall niche-filled building called a kaptar-khana. Scholars debate whether such buildings stored produce, housed pigeons, or served other purposes. Medieval real estate could include an unsolved outbuilding.

Measured houses commonly used a central corridor with rooms opening from it; larger examples added vestibules, stairs, storage, kitchens, and guest or ceremonial space. Hearths, tandoors, millstones, large jars, lamps, and animal remains reveal repeated work. Room labels are archaeological interpretations, not surviving family nameplates.

One well-preserved estate had plaster painted blue and red, a fired-brick floor arranged to resemble a carpet, and marble thresholds. Such decoration marks wealth and skilled work, not the average home. The same excavation also found storage pits and service spaces, reminding us that impressive floors still needed everyday sweeping.

The lower Oxus brought fertile silt through irrigation canals but could also shift channels and undermine towns. Kath’s history makes the river both provider and destroyer. Farming families depended on collective water management, yet the source does not tell us each worker’s legal status or how canal labor was divided by age or gender.

By the twelfth century, Khwarazm’s common rural house form grouped rooms around a central corridor and linked residence to farm space and storage. That pattern shows household production, not a universal menu or family size. Grain, recipe, appetite, feast, and hunger remain much harder to recover than walls.

Garden plots beside canals made irrigated produce possible around Khwarazmian estates. The archaeological plans do not list every crop or assign gardening to women, men, servants, or children. A canal-side garden is excellent evidence for cultivation and frustrating evidence for who weeded it, which is a very archaeological kind of joke.

The central-corridor house form included storage above or beside living space, helping households combine residence with farm management. Nerazik cautions that room counts do not translate directly into family counts. A large house might signal wealth, labor needs, an extended household, several phases, or some combination.

At Khwarazm’s court, Vatvat wrote diplomatic letters in Arabic to caliphal circles and in Persian to Sanjar and regional rulers. Couriers, scribes, paper, ink, and trained readers connected this oasis to distant courts. The archive illuminates elite communication; it does not measure literacy among farmers or herders.

The Oxus made exchange and farming possible, yet its silt and shifting channels could also move a town’s useful riverfront away. Boats, canal workers, farmers, and merchants depended on water that refused to read political maps. Khwarazm’s economy was connected to environmental maintenance as well as court decisions.

Nerazik proposed that extended-family organization may help explain some Khwarazmian house forms, but she explicitly rejected a mechanical equation between rooms and people. Patronymic groups, smaller units, servants, and changing occupancy could overlap. The responsible family portrait is therefore architectural possibility, not a confidently counted family tree.

House plans show places where people cooked, stored supplies, received guests, slept, worked, and climbed to upper rooms. They do not securely identify a nursery, classroom, or women’s quarter in every dwelling. Architectural function is reconstructed from installations and layout, not preserved room labels or family nameplates.

Children enter the learned medical record through a hygiene book that included childhood diseases, but no securely dated local toy group, school exercise, or first-person childhood account was identified for this polygon and century. Treatment categories are not children’s voices; work, play, discipline, and everyday learning remain evidence gaps.

Court assemblies offered a very elite kind of social life. Later anecdotes portray the small, sharp-tongued Vatvat answering jokes about his height and trading window-to-window wit with Atsiz. They are literary anecdotes, not transcripts, yet they preserve an enduring memory that verbal speed could be excellent armor at court.

The revolt account names leaders and collective branches but says little about women, marriage, elderly people, or family decision-making. We should not turn an army list into a society. Political sources make adult male chiefs unusually visible; the many people maintaining animals, food, shelter, kin ties, and migration logistics remain largely unnamed.

sections.title: Education, languages, and a written sample

items.text: Vatvat studied the Arabic philological tradition at Balkh’s Nezamiya madrasa before becoming a professional scribe in Khwarazm. That path documents advanced institutional education for one exceptionally successful man. It does not establish universal schools, literacy, or the curriculum of ordinary Oghuz children in camps or villages.

Mahmud of Kashgar’s eleventh-century dictionary compares its literary language with Oghuz speech and marks numerous entries as Oghuz. A modern study examines six such words: aŋ, etrek, keriş, könçek, sörçek, and yorıgçı. This is pre-1100 linguistic evidence preserved in a learned work, not a twelfth-century Oghuz manuscript.

No securely localized 1100 to 1200 vernacular Oghuz text from this polygon was identified for this packet. Spoken Oghuz, Khwarazmian, Persian, and other languages could meet in trade, service, and family life, but surviving dialect evidence comes through a learned dictionary. Absence from the archive is not absence of speech.

Written sample: “ای حریم صدر تو ترسندگان را چون حرم / از تو گشته بیضهٔ خوارزمشاهی محترم”. Transliteration: “Ey harim-e sadr-e to tarsandegān-rā chon haram / az to gašta beyża-ye Khwārazmšāhi mohtaram.” Translation: “O sanctuary of your seat, you are like sacred refuge to the fearful; through you the Khwarazmshah’s realm has become honored.”

The sample is Persian court panegyric addressed to Atsiz, so its place is the Khwarazmian court and its date is bounded by Atsiz’s 1127 to 1156 reign. The digital page transcribes a later edited divan, not an autograph. It demonstrates period court writing, not ordinary Oghuz pronunciation or mass literacy.

Jorjani served Qutb al-Din and Atsiz and produced the great Persian medical encyclopedia Zakhira-ye Khwarazmshahi plus a shorter work for Atsiz’s vizier. This is firm evidence for court-supported medicine in Khwarazm. It is not proof that camp families or poor farmers could consult a physician or own the books.

The encyclopedia organized anatomy, disease, hygiene and nutrition, diagnosis, fever, treatments, skin conditions, poisons, and drugs; its hygiene book included childhood, aging, and travel. Such structure is an intellectual achievement and a guide to learned concerns. It does not show how consistently recommendations became bedside practice.

Jorjani deliberately used many ordinary Persian body and illness words alongside Arabic scientific vocabulary. Examples discussed by Iranica include Persian terms for spleen, joints, kidney, wounds, inflammation, migraine, and bed-wetting. His vocabulary offers rare linguistic texture, while the treatments themselves belong to medieval Galenic medicine, not modern clinical advice.

A modern review calls Gorganch a medical center supported by Khwarazmshahs and lists multiple physicians, but it is a retrospective library study, not a hospital register. “School” here means a scholarly tradition and network. The evidence does not locate a public clinic, nursing system, vaccination program, or access rate for 1100 to 1200.

Khwarazmian houses contained tashnau-like soakaway or washing features, but this packet cannot securely label them toilets. Better-attested eleventh to twelfth-century toilet pipes, washing basins, drains, and soak wells come from comparison sites such as Otrar outside the polygon. The plumbing is real; its address matters. No flushing tent toilet is claimed.

Archaeology’s discovery is not a single gadget but a working landscape: roomed houses, farmyards, canals, mud construction, and debated towerlike buildings. Together they reveal skilled construction and intensive oasis life. They belong to Khwarazmian settlement history and should not be advertised as inventions of one Oghuz state.

The Oghuz victory in 1153 was a major military achievement for groups facing a sultan’s army, but its aftermath included plunder, death, displacement, and political breakdown. A child-friendly card can admire tactical success without making destruction cheerful. Winning a battle and building a safe society are different accomplishments.

Dehistan’s 1161 sack and later Khwarazmian campaigning show how quickly a frontier town could be fought over. The event is historically important without becoming an origin story for every ruin. Destruction, restoration, and ordinary occupation require different evidence, and surviving political reports illuminate the first much better than the others.

Court culture in Khwarazm produced bilingual correspondence, Persian poetry, philology, and medical writing. Those achievements grew within an irrigated, multilingual oasis court whose rulers also fought steppe neighbors. The cultural record is rich but socially narrow; farmers, herders, builders, patients, and waste handlers wrote far fewer surviving biographies.

At 1200 the target disappears. Former tested oasis points move to the Qara Khitai layer, while Ustyurt and Caspian-side points move to Cuman layers; by 1279 the same area is divided again. These software transitions summarize different map regimes. They are not proof of one conquest, one successor, or population replacement.

ending.text: The “oghuz” feature ends at the atlas’s 1200 seam, not at a demonstrated Oghuz collapse. Former tested oasis points move into the Qara Khitai layer, while Ustyurt and Caspian-side points enter Cuman layers. The label vanishes even though communities and political histories continue. No single successor can honestly inherit this geographic and historical collage.
